paragraphs: The paper describes a neural network for strengthening and completing visually prominent closed contours. Its starting point is unusual: the input consists of spots without a preferred orientation, rather than already identified edges. The authors relate this choice to the kind of input that reaches the visual area V1 from the LGN.

The network’s computation is defined through a probability distribution over closed contours generated by a random process. This gives contour enhancement a precise mathematical target. The network is computing a specified function of the input, making its behavior interpretable in terms of the underlying contour distribution.

A central result concerns geometric invariance. Although the network itself is discrete, its output is invariant to continuous rotations and translations of the input pattern. This connects a practical representational choice with a strong geometric property: contour saliency does not depend on a particular position or orientation. Together, the spot-based input, probabilistic definition, and invariance distinguish the proposed approach.
neurips-2001-a-rotation-and-translation-.tldr: A discrete neural network enhances and completes closed contours from spot-based input while preserving invariance to continuous rotations and translations.

paragraphs: The head-direction system must convert signals about how quickly the head is turning into a representation of its direction. This requires integration: accumulating changes in angle over time. In several brain regions, direction is represented by neurons that fire most strongly when the head points toward their preferred direction.

The difficulty is that head movements span a wide range of speeds. Earlier models used a ring-shaped attractor network described through firing rates, but accurate integration during fast rotations required very fast synaptic dynamics. The paper asks whether integration can instead work with slow synapses, including excitatory NMDA and inhibitory GABA(B) types.

For networks with such slow synapses, firing-rate dynamics provide a good approximation to spiking neurons. Within this setting, the authors find that accurate integration at high rotation speeds places strong constraints on network architecture. The contribution is therefore an architectural constraint on proposed mechanisms: a plausible account must accommodate both slow synaptic responses and rapid changes in head direction.
neurips-2001-a-theory-of-neural-integrat.tldr: Accurately integrating rapid head turns with slow synapses places strong constraints on the architecture of head-direction networks.

paragraphs: The paper studies how to find compounds that bind to a target molecule while using as few rounds of biological testing as possible. Each round tests only a small batch from a much larger collection. Active learning addresses the resulting selection problem by using existing test outcomes to choose the next batch.

The authors compare three strategies. One selects compounds close to a maximum-margin decision boundary. Another trains perceptrons using different orderings of the data and selects compounds whose predicted labels receive the most evenly divided votes. The third considers the set of weight vectors consistent with observed labels, estimates how evenly a compound would divide that set, and favors balanced divisions.

These strategies use different representations of uncertainty to decide which measurements to request. On two datasets supplied by DuPont Pharmaceuticals, all three perform comparably and substantially outperform random batch selection. The finding supports targeted selection in the tested discovery setting: the choice of compounds for testing can materially improve the search process.
neurips-2001-active-learning-in-the-drug.tldr: Three active learning strategies select compound-testing batches comparably well and substantially outperform random selection on two pharmaceutical datasets.

paragraphs: Nearest-neighbor classification relies on nearby examples having approximately constant class probabilities. With many input dimensions and only finitely many examples, that local assumption becomes unreliable because of the curse of dimensionality. The paper addresses this problem by changing how distance is measured around the point being classified.

The proposed method uses a support vector machine to construct a locally flexible metric. Its maximum-margin boundary identifies the direction that best distinguishes classes within the query’s neighborhood. That direction then determines local weights for the input features, so the neighborhood used for classification reflects the local discrimination problem.

This combines a boundary-based learning method with neighborhood-based prediction. The support vector machine supplies information about which local differences matter, and the nearest-neighbor procedure uses that information in its distance calculation. Experiments on simulated and real datasets show improved classification performance over an SVM alone and several adaptive learning schemes. These are empirical improvements in the evaluated settings, supporting locally learned distance as a useful component of classification.
neurips-2001-adaptive-nearest-neighbor-c.tldr: Using a local SVM boundary to weight features improves nearest-neighbor classification in experiments on simulated and real data.

paragraphs: Speech recognition becomes difficult when loud noise changes substantially during an utterance. One approach estimates clean speech features before passing them to a recognizer trained on clean speech. The authors’ earlier method combined separate probability models of speech and noise, using an iterative second-order Taylor approximation for inference.

The new contribution is learning the noise model directly from an utterance that also contains speech. This matters when isolated noise examples are unavailable, or when speech-free portions fail to capture noise changes throughout the utterance. The same test utterance supplies the information for adapting the noise model and is then denoised using that model.

The method uses approximate inference as the expectation step within a generalized EM procedure for learning noise parameters. On Wall Street Journal speech with added noise and on the Aurora benchmark, the adaptive method performs as well as or significantly better than the nonadaptive method. These results support adaptation without a separate noise-training collection, including settings where noise cannot be estimated adequately from silent intervals.
neurips-2001-algonquin-learning-dynamic-.tldr: ALGONQUIN learns a changing noise model from the test utterance itself, matching or improving nonadaptive performance without separate noise-training examples.

paragraphs: Cobot is a software agent operating inside the online community LambdaMOO. Its earlier role was to collect social statistics and report them to users. This paper extends that role through reinforcement learning, allowing the agent to take proactive actions and adapt its behavior using rewards and punishments supplied by community members.

The learning setting involves multiple human sources of feedback rather than a single fixed evaluator. The paper describes the environment together with Cobot’s state and action spaces, which specify what situations it distinguishes and what actions it can take. Its behavior can therefore change according to its current state as learning proceeds.

After five months, Cobot had received 3,171 reward and punishment events from 254 users. The authors report that it learned nontrivial preferences for a number of users and modified its behavior according to its state. This is evidence of adaptation within a working social environment. The result shows how reinforcement learning can extend an informational community agent into one whose actions respond to accumulated human feedback.
neurips-2001-cobot-a-social-reinforcemen.tldr: Cobot learned state-dependent social behavior from rewards and punishments supplied by users of an online community.

paragraphs: Neural population codes often describe a stimulus through how each neuron’s average response changes with it. Long-range correlations can greatly suppress the information available in those averages. This paper investigates a different source of information: second-order response statistics, which describe response variability and relationships between fluctuations.

The authors show that Fisher information in the studied system grows linearly with population size. Fisher information measures how sensitively the response distribution distinguishes nearby stimulus values. Linear growth means that increasing the number of neurons increases this measure proportionally within the system being analyzed.

The paper also proposes a bilinear readout for extracting information from the code and evaluates it on discrimination and estimation tasks. Its central interpretation is that stimulus-dependent changes in individual neurons’ response variances supply the main information source. Thus, although the work concerns correlation codes, the reported information is primarily carried by how each neuron’s variability changes with the stimulus. This clarifies both where information resides and how a readout might access it.
neurips-2001-correlation-codes-in-neuron.tldr: The studied second-order population code gains Fisher information linearly with population size, mainly through stimulus-dependent single-neuron variances.

paragraphs: The paper addresses clustering data whose appearance changes under transformations such as rotation, scaling, or translation. Earlier transformed mixture models jointly learned clusters and normalized observations through EM. Their inputs were the data, a list of allowable transformations, and the desired number of clusters, but exhaustive transformation calculations limited scalability.

The new approach combines a variational method that decouples transformations with a fast Fourier transform method for posterior calculations. For square images with side length N and N choices for each of four transformations, the stated per-iteration cost falls from C times N to the sixth power to N squared times the quantity C plus twice log N, for C clusters.

The authors demonstrate a four-component mixture on video frames measuring 320 by 240 pixels, accounting for 360 rotations and 76,800 translations. Each EM iteration takes ten seconds per frame in MATLAB, reported as over five million times faster than the original algorithm. This demonstrates a substantial computational improvement for the specified example, making a previously expensive transformation search more practical.
neurips-2001-fast-large-scale-transforma.tldr: Variational decoupling and Fourier-transform calculations dramatically reduce the cost of jointly clustering images and accounting for transformations.

paragraphs: High-dimensional observations can lie near a surface with far fewer underlying dimensions. A collection of local linear models can describe separate parts of that surface, but those models need not share compatible coordinates. Moving between their regions can therefore fail to provide a coherent global description of the data.

The paper represents the local models as a mixture of factor analyzers and adds a regularization term to maximum-likelihood learning. The regularizer favors consistent alignment of their internal coordinate systems. It resolves a freedom in the mixture’s parameterization that otherwise permits locally valid but mutually uncoordinated representations.

The resulting internal coordinates vary smoothly and continuously along connected paths on the manifold, including paths crossing several local models. The regularizer is expressed as a Kullback-Leibler divergence. This gives variational methods a representation-learning role: they help choose useful internal coordinates even though the probabilistic models already permit tractable inference. The contribution links local statistical descriptions to a coordinated representation of the overall manifold.
neurips-2001-global-coordination-of-loca.tldr: A KL-divergence regularizer aligns local factor-analyzer coordinates into a smooth global representation of a data manifold.

paragraphs: Learning statistical grammar from unlabeled text can require computations that become impractical on large datasets. This paper addresses that obstacle by proposing a simpler probabilistic model of English grammar. The aim is to retain a useful representation of syntax while making unsupervised training computationally manageable.

The model is organized around grammatical bigrams: syntactic relationships between pairs of words. These pairwise relationships provide the building blocks for its grammar representation. The simplified structure admits an efficient expectation-maximization training algorithm, connecting the representational choice directly to the feasibility of learning from large amounts of text.

The experiments examine three distinct questions: how adequately the model represents grammar, how well it generalizes from labeled examples, and whether it can induce syntactic structure from raw text. Together, these evaluations address the usefulness of the representation as well as its learnability. The contribution is a tractable grammar-modeling approach with empirical assessment along these dimensions; the abstract does not characterize the reported results as uniformly successful or superior to conventional models.
neurips-2001-grammatical-bigrams-3e980a1.tldr: A simpler grammar model built from pairwise syntactic relationships enables efficient EM training and is evaluated on representation and learning tasks.

paragraphs: The paper extends mixture-of-experts modeling by making each expert a Gaussian process regression model. A gating mechanism determines how experts participate as the input changes. This arrangement lets the overall predictor combine Gaussian process models through an input-dependent structure.

The gating network uses an input-dependent adaptation of the Dirichlet process to accommodate an infinite number of experts. The authors describe inference through a Markov chain based on Gibbs sampling and state that this can be done efficiently. The model therefore combines flexibility in the expert collection with a sampling-based procedure for working with it.

One consequence is that the effective covariance function can vary with the inputs, allowing the overall model’s statistical relationships to differ across input locations. The authors also suggest that the approach may handle large datasets, potentially addressing another major difficulty of Gaussian processes. Simulations demonstrate viability. The findings support the construction as a promising modeling approach, while its large-dataset capability is presented as a possibility rather than an established general guarantee.
neurips-2001-infinite-mixtures-of-gaussi.tldr: An input-dependent infinite mixture of Gaussian process experts enables varying covariance structure and may improve handling of large datasets.

paragraphs: Likelihood-ratio classification compares how strongly competing classes explain an observation. Estimated ratios can differ from the true ratios, affecting the resulting decisions. This paper introduces an information-theoretic correction term for multiclass classification and analyzes its behavior in the Gaussian case.

Under certain conditions, the correction is sufficient to optimally compensate for the difference between the estimated and true likelihood ratio. Adding it also changes the structure of class comparisons: the comparisons can become intransitive, meaning their preferences need not form a consistent overall ranking. The authors investigate tournament-like procedures for turning those comparisons into classification decisions.

On medium-vocabulary speech recognition tasks, the correction significantly improves classification results. An appropriate tournament produces additional, smaller improvements. The authors also find that intransitivity appears useful as a measure of classification confidence. The work therefore connects three issues: correcting imperfect likelihood estimates, resolving potentially inconsistent pairwise comparisons, and using their structure to assess confidence. Its optimal-correction statement remains conditional, while the performance improvements are findings from the reported speech tasks.
neurips-2001-intransitive-likelihood-rat.tldr: An information-theoretic likelihood-ratio correction improves speech classification, with tournament strategies providing smaller additional gains when comparisons become intransitive.

paragraphs: The paper studies how a neural population can be decoded repeatedly while retaining information from an earlier estimate. At each step, the estimated stimulus from the previous step supplies prior knowledge for the next decoding operation. This makes the decoding process sequential, with earlier inference contributing to the interpretation of subsequent population activity.

The decoder uses maximum a posteriori estimation: it selects the stimulus estimate favored after combining current evidence with the prior. The authors analyze the accuracy of this Bayesian decoding scheme. The question is therefore both computational, concerning estimation accuracy, and biological, concerning how neural circuitry could perform the operation.

The proposed implementation is a biologically plausible recurrent network. Prior knowledge is conveyed through changes in recurrent interactions produced by Hebbian learning. This connects a probabilistic ingredient—the prior—to an adaptable property of the network itself. The result shows that the studied Bayesian decoder can be implemented through such recurrent interactions, providing a concrete link between sequential population decoding and a neural learning mechanism.
neurips-2001-neural-implementation-of-ba.tldr: A recurrent network can implement sequential Bayesian population decoding by encoding prior estimates through Hebbian changes in recurrent interactions.

paragraphs: The paper proposes a way to bound a classifier’s true error rate using PAC-Bayes theory. Its starting point is sensitivity: how much does the model’s behavior change when noise is added to each parameter? This information is used to construct a distribution over classifiers from a continuous-valued model.

The resulting object is a stochastic classifier defined through that distribution. A PAC-Bayes bound is then applied to its true error rate. The sensitivity analysis and the bound serve complementary roles: the analysis determines the classifier distribution, and the bound provides an error guarantee for the stochastic classifier that results.

The authors demonstrate the method on artificial neural networks and report substantially tighter bounds than the best deterministic neural-network bounds used in their comparison. The supplied text does not preserve the numerical improvement clearly. The essential distinction is that the reported guarantee concerns the stochastic classifier constructed by the method. The contribution is a route from parameter sensitivity to informative error bounds through a distribution over models.
neurips-2001-not-bounding-the-true-error.tldr: Parameter-noise sensitivity guides a stochastic classifier construction whose PAC-Bayes error bounds substantially improve on compared deterministic neural-network bounds.

paragraphs: The Cluster Variation Method is a family of approximation methods that includes the Bethe and Kikuchi approximations. The paper develops two new iterative schemes within this family. Its focus is on making these approximations useful for inference problems through concrete procedures for computing their solutions.

The first scheme uses fixed-point iteration, repeatedly applying an update toward a state that reproduces itself. On directed graphical models, the authors report significant improvement over loopy belief propagation, mean-field methods, and TAP methods. This is a performance finding for the evaluated class of models rather than a universal ordering of inference techniques.

The second scheme is gradient based and comes with a convergence guarantee. It also produces useful results on random graphs with mild frustration, which is the stated setting for that empirical finding. Together, the methods contribute different advantages: improved results in the directed-model comparison and guaranteed convergence for the gradient procedure. The authors conclude that these developments have substantial practical value for large inference problems.
neurips-2001-novel-iteration-schemes-for.tldr: Two Cluster Variation Method algorithms offer improved directed-model inference and, for the gradient-based scheme, guaranteed convergence.

paragraphs: A product-of-experts model combines several probability models by multiplying their contributions into one distribution. This paper studies Gaussian experts. Their normalized product is also Gaussian, but combining individually simple covariance structures can produce a richer overall structure. Gaussian experts make this architecture especially amenable to mathematical analysis.

One construction uses Gaussian pancakes: distributions compressed along one direction and extended along the remaining directions. The authors show that maximum-likelihood learning of their product yields a probabilistic formulation of Minor Components Analysis. This complements the probabilistic formulation of Principal Components Analysis and connects the geometry of individual experts to a familiar component-analysis method.

The paper also examines products of one-factor probabilistic PCA models and a product-of-experts construction for a first-order autoregressive process. Across these examples, the central issue is how simple expert structures combine into an overall Gaussian model. The supplied derivation expresses this combination through addition of inverse covariance matrices, making the relationship between each expert’s constraints and the resulting distribution explicit.
neurips-2001-products-of-gaussians-f4455.tldr: Products of simple Gaussian experts yield richer Gaussian structures, including a maximum-likelihood formulation of probabilistic Minor Components Analysis.

paragraphs: The paper proposes an unsupervised framework for learning projection models through density estimation on quantized sample spaces. Its objective is to preserve the data’s probability density. This changes how the quantizer is chosen: the criterion concerns reconstructing the distribution, rather than optimally reconstructing individual observations.

The resulting model is called a quantizing density estimator. The authors provide a general method for estimating its parameters and selecting a model. They also show how projection sets associated with established methods, including vector quantization and principal component analysis, fit within the framework. This connects familiar representations to a density-focused learning objective.

Experiments with a principal component quantizer use both synthetic and real-world data. They show that the quantizing density estimator can improve generalization over a kernel density estimator, despite relying on substantially lower-dimensional projection indices. The significance is that retaining fewer representational coordinates can still support a better estimate of the underlying density in the tested settings. The finding is a demonstrated possibility, rather than a guarantee for every projection or dataset.
neurips-2001-quantizing-density-estimato.tldr: Choosing quantized projections to preserve probability density can improve density-estimation generalization while using much lower-dimensional representations.

paragraphs: The paper begins with an interpretation of logistic units in a feedforward network’s first hidden layer: they compute a data point’s relative probability under two Gaussian models. This suggests treating the unit’s computation as a comparison between density models, opening a path to substitute other kinds of probabilistic models.

The authors use this idea to construct a network of many small hidden Markov models. The architecture supports discriminative learning of HMMs and connects that learning to a neural-network formulation. Its distinctive design choice is to use multiple small sequence models as components of a larger discriminative architecture.

Experiments on speech data show the architecture outperforming the standard method of discriminatively training HMMs used in the comparison. The result supports the relative-density construction as a useful way to organize speech models in the tested setting. More broadly, the paper’s conceptual contribution is the connection between a familiar neural computation and density comparison: changing the probabilistic models inside that comparison leads to a different trainable architecture.
neurips-2001-relative-density-nets-a-new.tldr: A relative-density interpretation of logistic units motivates a network of small HMMs that improves discriminative speech modeling in the reported experiments.

paragraphs: Many classification problems provide abundant observations but labels for only a small fraction of them. The paper extends boosting to this semi-supervised setting through the optimization framework of MarginBoost. The aim is to let the learning procedure make use of unlabeled examples alongside labeled ones.

The central step is extending the definition of a margin to unlabeled data. From the resulting margin-based cost, the authors derive a gradient descent algorithm. This ties the semi-supervised extension to an explicit optimization objective, rather than simply adding unlabeled observations to a procedure designed only for labeled examples.

The resulting meta-learning scheme can work with any base classifier capable of benefiting from unlabeled data. The paper instantiates it using mixture models trained by expectation-maximization. Benchmark experiments vary the proportion of labeled observations and produce results the authors describe as promising. The contribution is therefore both a general boosting framework and a concrete demonstration, with its applicability depending on the base learner’s ability to use the unlabeled portion of the data.
neurips-2001-semi-supervised-marginboost.tldr: Semi-supervised MarginBoost extends margins to unlabeled examples and derives a boosting procedure for base learners that can use them.

paragraphs: Online reinforcement learning can fail to converge when value functions are approximated. The paper addresses this by separating experience collection from function fitting. Its Batch Fit to Best Paths algorithm alternates between exploration and a batch learning phase, giving each phase a distinct role.

During exploration, the agent generates trajectories intended to uncover fragments of an optimal policy. During fitting, a function approximator learns from the best known paths connecting start states to terminal states. Batch fitting considers the approximation problem globally, allowing it to address tradeoffs that local online updates cannot handle.

The approach builds on earlier incremental-batch methods by improving exploration and adding Bellman-error and advantage-error measures to the fitting objective. These changes enrich the criteria used to fit the value function, alongside information from successful paths. Results show better performance on several benchmark problems. The evidence supports the revised exploration and fitting strategy in those tasks; the abstract’s stated outcome is improved performance, rather than a general proof that every instance converges.
neurips-2001-stabilizing-value-function-.tldr: BFBP alternates exploration with batch fitting to the best known paths, improving performance on several reinforcement-learning benchmarks.

paragraphs: The paper derives an adaptive TAP Gibbs free energy for a broad class of densely connected probabilistic models. The class has quadratic interactions and allows arbitrary constraints at individual sites. The free-energy formulation provides a mathematical objective for developing approximation algorithms within this specified modeling setting.

The authors then show that a particular sequential minimization of this objective leads to a generalization of expectation propagation. This establishes a connection between the free-energy construction and an existing approximate-inference approach. The update procedure follows from how the objective is minimized, giving the algorithm a common organizing principle.

A further derivation produces a version of the sequential algorithm using a sparse representation. The authors demonstrate the approach on Gaussian-process classification, Gaussian-process density estimation, and an independent component analysis problem. These applications show its usefulness across several tasks. The contribution combines a theoretical objective, an associated sequential inference procedure, and a sparse formulation, with the modeling scope grounded in the stated interaction structure and single-site constraints.
neurips-2001-tap-gibbs-free-energy-belie.tldr: An adaptive TAP free-energy formulation yields a generalized expectation-propagation algorithm and a sparse version demonstrated on several probabilistic learning tasks.

paragraphs: The Concave-Convex Procedure is a general framework for constructing iterative optimization algorithms. It produces discrete-time updates with a guarantee that the chosen optimization or energy function decreases monotonically. This gives the generated procedure a clear relationship to the objective it is intended to optimize.

The authors describe the framework as applicable to almost any optimization problem and show that many existing algorithms can be understood through it. They prove relationships with some applications of Legendre transform techniques. This makes CCCP useful for interpreting established methods as well as for designing new update rules.

The paper illustrates the framework through Potts models, linear assignment, expectation-maximization algorithms, and Generalized Iterative Scaling. These examples show how the same optimization perspective reaches across different problems and procedures. The key guarantee is monotonic reduction of the objective; that statement should not be read as a promise of finding a global optimum. Its significance is a shared construction principle that connects algorithm design with controlled progress in an energy function.
neurips-2001-the-concave-convex-procedur.tldr: CCCP provides a broad framework for deriving and understanding iterative algorithms whose objective values decrease monotonically.

paragraphs: The paper studies reinforcement learning with several goals in an initially unknown dynamic environment. Some environmental changes may vary arbitrarily because of other agents or nonstationary external influences. The authors model this as a stochastic game between the learner and an arbitrary player, with each outcome producing a vector of rewards.

The learner’s objective is for its long-run average reward vector to belong to a specified target set. This expresses success through several reward components together. The proposed algorithm draws on approachability theory for stochastic games and appropriately combines a finite collection of standard learning algorithms that each use scalar rewards.

The authors provide sufficient conditions for convergence to a general target set. These conditions establish when the steering construction succeeds, without claiming success for every environment or target. They also discuss the specialization to a single-controller Markov decision problem. The contribution is a way to build a multiple-goal learning procedure from scalar learners while retaining a conditional theoretical account of its long-run behavior.
neurips-2001-the-steering-approach-for-m.tldr: A steering algorithm combines scalar-reward learners to approach a target set of average reward vectors under sufficient convergence conditions.

paragraphs: Transform-invariant image models had shown strong results for collections of objects with similar appearances. This paper seeks to extend that capability to object classes whose individual members vary considerably, such as pedestrians. The challenge is to represent shared class structure despite changes in the appearance of particular instances.

The proposed representation uses pixel-wise similarities, called similarity templates. It is invariant to the particular colors of an object’s components, allowing the model to capture relationships that persist when those colors differ. According to the authors, this representation enables both detection of class instances and alignment of those instances.

The model also implicitly represents regions of color regularity across the class-specific image collection. That structure enables decomposition of the object class into component regions. Detection, alignment, and decomposition are therefore connected through the same similarity-based representation. The contribution is a way to describe recurring visual organization across varying instances, using shared patterns of pixel similarity rather than requiring particular components to retain the same colors.
neurips-2001-transform-invariant-image-d.tldr: Similarity templates use pixel-wise relationships to detect, align, and decompose object classes despite variation in component colors.

paragraphs: Computing marginal probabilities in graphs containing cycles often requires approximation. This paper introduces a tree-based reparameterization view of iterative inference algorithms. Belief propagation fits within the framework as a very local reparameterization method, while broader algorithms perform exact computations on spanning trees of the full graph.

The authors find that these tree reparameterization algorithms have better convergence properties than belief propagation in practice. The framework also supplies theoretical insights: a new characterization of fixed points and an invariance shared by tree reparameterization and belief propagation. These properties allow analysis and bounds on the discrepancy between approximate and actual marginals.

Much of the analysis extends beyond the particular algorithm used to obtain an approximation. Most results apply to any local minimum of the Bethe free energy, and the authors describe natural extensions to more structured approximations. The contribution is therefore both computational and explanatory: tree-based updates offer practical convergence advantages, while reparameterization provides tools for understanding the solutions and errors of a broader family of inference procedures.
neurips-2001-tree-based-reparameterizati.tldr: Tree-based reparameterization unifies approximate-inference algorithms, improves convergence empirically, and enables analysis of fixed points and marginal errors.
